summary: Solving problems with numbers to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and depends on careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points, equalising lengths by padding with zeros (1.5 = 1.500), reading each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. 'Find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercises complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000). Estimating first guards against place-value slips.
misconceptions: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point (1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199)
Treats the decimal tail as a separate whole number ('longer is larger')
Forgets to pad and borrow across the point (1.5 − 0.375)
Complement-to-1 errors: completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the required 3 d.p. (0.4 + 0.6)

activities.title: Column workbench: aligning and padding to thousandths
steps: Set out the subtraction 1.5 − 0.375 in place-value columns (ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths) aligned on the decimal point — the measuring context is a 1.5-litre bottle from which 0.375 l is poured out, finding how much is left.
Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500 by writing zeros in the empty hundredths and thousandths columns before subtracting.
Carry out the subtraction, borrowing just as with whole numbers (from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths), to reach 1.125 l remaining.
Add the three ragged measurements 1.2 m + 0.567 m + 2.233 m by first aligning on the point and padding every number to the same length (1.2 = 1.200), then summing each column to get 4.000 m.
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) and check the answer's size against the estimate.
activities.insight: 1.5 and 1.500 are the same number, but writing the padding zeros makes the hundredths and thousandths columns available so the digits line up and the borrow can ripple from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths.

activities.title: Make 1: complements to a whole at three decimal places
steps: Given 0.375, find the second number to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.000, by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625).
Check the pair by adding the two numbers back together and confirming they total exactly 1.000.
Explain why 0.4 + 0.6, though it equals 1, does not meet the 'three decimal places' requirement, and give a valid 3-d.p. pair (such as 0.001 + 0.999).
Optionally model the complement as two lengths placed end to end along a bar representing one whole, where only the correct pair closes the gap with no gap or overlap and a running total shows 1.000.
activities.insight: A complement to 1 is found by subtracting from the whole written as 1.000, not by completing each column to 10 independently; the two parts together must make exactly one whole.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Show me your method for each. First, add 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m. Second, a 1.5-litre bottle has 0.375 litres poured out — how much is left? Third, find two numbers, each with three decimal places, that add up to exactly 1.' Watch how they line the numbers up and handle the borrow.
